claim: The central amygdala (CeA) is an important brain region for regulating both negative (fear and anxiety) and positive (reward) affective behaviors.
source: The central amygdala (CeA) has emerged as an important brain region for regulating both negative (fear and anxiety) and positive (reward) affective behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing the CeA's role in affective behaviors.

claim: The CeA has been proposed to encode affective information in the form of valence (whether the stimulus is good or bad) or salience (how significant is the stimulus).
source: The CeA has been proposed to encode affective information in the form of valence (whether the stimulus is good or bad) or salience (how significant is the stimulus), but the extent to which these two types of stimulus representation occur in the CeA is not known.
evidence: This claim is based on prior theoretical proposals in the literature about CeA encoding.

claim: The extent to which valence and salience encoding occur in the CeA is not known.
source: The CeA has been proposed to encode affective information in the form of valence (whether the stimulus is good or bad) or salience (how significant is the stimulus), but the extent to which these two types of stimulus representation occur in the CeA is not known.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Approximately 65% of CeA neurons encode the valence of the unconditioned stimulus (US).
source: Here, we used single cell calcium imaging in mice during appetitive and aversive conditioning and found that majority of CeA neurons (~65%) encode the valence of the unconditioned stimulus (US) with a smaller subset of cells (~15%) encoding the salience of the US.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single cell calcium imaging during conditioning.

claim: Approximately 15% of CeA neurons encode the salience of the unconditioned stimulus (US).
source: Here, we used single cell calcium imaging in mice during appetitive and aversive conditioning and found that majority of CeA neurons (~65%) encode the valence of the unconditioned stimulus (US) with a smaller subset of cells (~15%) encoding the salience of the US.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single cell calcium imaging during conditioning.

claim: Valence and salience encoding of the conditioned stimulus (CS) was observed, albeit to a lesser extent than US encoding.
source: Valence and salience encoding of the conditioned stimulus (CS) was also observed, albeit to a lesser extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CS and US responses.

claim: The CeA is a site of convergence for encoding oppositely valenced US information.
source: These findings show that the CeA is a site of convergence for encoding oppositely valenced US information.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that CeA neurons respond to both appetitive and aversive stimuli.

claim: The CeA is comprised of multiple genetically distinct cell types that contribute to both appetitive and aversive processes.
source: The CeA is comprised of multiple genetically distinct cell types that contribute to both appetitive and aversive processes (Cai et al., 2014; Douglass et al., 2017; Fadok et al., 2018; Hardaway et al., 2019; Haubensak et al., 2010; Isosaka et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013; McCullough et al., 2018; Warlow et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Subsets of cells in the CeA encode conditioned and/or unconditioned fear stimulus information.
source: Subsets of cells in the CeA encode conditioned and/or unconditioned fear stimulus information (Ciocchi et al., 2010; Duvarci et al., 2011; Fadok et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013; Sanford et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2017), as well as appetitive information (Douglass et al., 2017; Hardaway et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Subsets of cells in the CeA encode appetitive information.
source: Subsets of cells in the CeA encode conditioned and/or unconditioned fear stimulus information (Ciocchi et al., 2010; Duvarci et al., 2011; Fadok et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013; Sanford et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2017), as well as appetitive information (Douglass et al., 2017; Hardaway et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Plasticity within neurons of the CeA contributes to both fear-related learning and reward-associated learning.
source: Plasticity within neurons of the CeA (Fu and Shinnick-Gallagher, 2005) contributes to both fear-related learning (Li et al., 2013; Penzo et al., 2014; Sanford et al., 2017) and reward-associated learning (Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cells implicated in fear processing have been shown to regulate consummatory behaviors.
source: Cells implicated in fear processing have also been shown to regulate consummatory behaviors (Cai et al., 2014; Douglass et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2017), suggesting that subsets of CeA neurons encode either incentive salience (the significance of the stimulus regardless of valence) or valence (whether it is a positive or negative outcome).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Subsets of CeA neurons encode either incentive salience or valence.
source: Cells implicated in fear processing have also been shown to regulate consummatory behaviors (Cai et al., 2014; Douglass et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2017), suggesting that subsets of CeA neurons encode either incentive salience (the significance of the stimulus regardless of valence) or valence (whether it is a positive or negative outcome).
evidence: This claim is inferred from prior literature showing that fear-processing cells also regulate consummatory behaviors.

claim: Specific subsets of neurons within the CeA contribute to multiple aspects of appetitive and aversive behaviors.
source: Specific subsets of neurons within the CeA have been shown to contribute to multiple aspects of appetitive and aversive behaviors (Balleine and Killcross, 2006; Kong and Zweifel, 2021; Pignatelli and Beyeler, 2019) and it was recently shown that subpopulations of CeA neurons provide scalar signals to oppositely valenced stimuli to promote learning (Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Subpopulations of CeA neurons provide scalar signals to oppositely valenced stimuli to promote learning.
source: Specific subsets of neurons within the CeA have been shown to contribute to multiple aspects of appetitive and aversive behaviors (Balleine and Killcross, 2006; Kong and Zweifel, 2021; Pignatelli and Beyeler, 2019) and it was recently shown that subpopulations of CeA neurons provide scalar signals to oppositely valenced stimuli to promote learning (Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The full extent to which the CeA encodes the salience or valence of positive and negative affective information remains unresolved.
source: However, the full extent to which the CeA encodes the salience or valence of positive and negative affective information remains unresolved.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: GCaMP6m was selectively expressed in GABAergic neurons of VgatIRES-Cre mice.
source: To monitor calcium dynamics in CeA neurons during positive and negative reinforcement, we selectively expressed GCaMP6m in GABAergic neurons of VgatIRES-Cre (Slc32a1tm2(cre)Lowl/J; JAX strain #: 016962) mice (4 males and 6 females) and implanted a gradient-index (GRIN) lens in the CeA (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: A gradient-index (GRIN) lens was implanted in the CeA for calcium imaging.
source: To monitor calcium dynamics in CeA neurons during positive and negative reinforcement, we selectively expressed GCaMP6m in GABAergic neurons of VgatIRES-Cre (Slc32a1tm2(cre)Lowl/J; JAX strain #: 016962) mice (4 males and 6 females) and implanted a gradient-index (GRIN) lens in the CeA (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Mice were conditioned in both Pavlovian appetitive and Pavlovian fear paradigms, with the conditioning order counterbalanced.
source: Mice were conditioned in both Pavlovian appetitive and Pavlovian fear paradigms, with the conditioning order counterbalanced (Figure 1B, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: During appetitive learning, mice demonstrated a significant increase in time spent near the food hopper during the food-predicting CS (CSFood).
source: During appetitive learning, mice demonstrated a significant increase in time spent near the food hopper during the food-predicting CS (CSFood), reduced latency to retrieve the food pellet, and an increased success rate in procuring the reward (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During appetitive learning, mice showed reduced latency to retrieve the food pellet.
source: During appetitive learning, mice demonstrated a significant increase in time spent near the food hopper during the food-predicting CS (CSFood), reduced latency to retrieve the food pellet, and an increased success rate in procuring the reward (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During appetitive learning, mice showed an increased success rate in procuring the reward.
source: During appetitive learning, mice demonstrated a significant increase in time spent near the food hopper during the food-predicting CS (CSFood), reduced latency to retrieve the food pellet, and an increased success rate in procuring the reward (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During fear conditioning, animals learned that the shock-predicting CS (CSShock) was followed by an impending foot shock and displayed increased freezing behavior to the CSShock as trials progressed.
source: During fear conditioning, the animals learned that the shock-predicting CS (CSShock) was followed by an impending foot shock and displayed increased freezing behavior to the CSShock as trials progressed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Responsive and non-responsive cells to both the appetitive and aversive US were observed during conditioning.
source: During conditioning, we observed responsive and non-responsive cells to both the appetitive and aversive US (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A variation of the 'circular shift' method was developed to stringently define cells with statistically significant responses.
source: To resolve event-related calcium signals, we developed a variation of the 'circular shift' method27 to stringently define cells with statistically significant responses (see Methods for detailed description).
evidence: This claim describes the statistical method developed for the study.

claim: On day 1 of Pavlovian appetitive conditioning, no responsive cells to the CSFood or food delivery were identified.
source: During Pavlovian appetitive conditioning, alignment to the cue presentation revealed no responsive cells to the CSFood or food delivery on day 1 (Figure 3A, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: On day 10 of Pavlovian appetitive conditioning, numerous cells were identified that were responsive to food delivery with either increases or decreases in calcium signals.
source: However, on day 10, numerous cells were identified that were responsive to food delivery with either increases or decreases in calcium signals (Figure 3A, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Analysis of responses aligned to food retrieval (head entry) revealed responsive cells on both day 1 and day 10.
source: Analysis of responses aligned to food retrieval (head entry) revealed responsive cells on both day 1 and day 10 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The number of cells showing increased calcium to head entry and the magnitude of the increase was larger on day 10 compared to day 1.
source: The number of cells showing increased calcium to head entry and the magnitude of the increase was larger on day 10 compared to day 1 (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Of the 872 cells recorded on day 10 of conditioning, a small proportion of cells were responsive to CSFood presentation, showing similar proportions of cells with increased or decreased calcium signals.
source: Of the 872 cells recorded on day 10 of conditioning, a small proportion of cells were responsive to CSFood presentation, showing similar proportions of cells with increased or decreased calcium signals (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: Of the CSFood responsive cells, the majority were responsive to both the CS and the food delivery.
source: Of these CSFood responsive cells, the majority were responsive to both the CS and the food delivery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 64% of CeA neurons were responsive to food delivery on day 10 of appetitive conditioning.
source: In contrast to the CSFood responsive cells, a large number (64%) of CeA neurons were responsive to food delivery, with the largest proportion of cells showing excitatory responses (40%) compared to inhibited responses (24%) (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: 40% of CeA neurons showed excitatory responses to food delivery on day 10 of appetitive conditioning.
source: In contrast to the CSFood responsive cells, a large number (64%) of CeA neurons were responsive to food delivery, with the largest proportion of cells showing excitatory responses (40%) compared to inhibited responses (24%) (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: 24% of CeA neurons showed inhibited responses to food delivery on day 10 of appetitive conditioning.
source: In contrast to the CSFood responsive cells, a large number (64%) of CeA neurons were responsive to food delivery, with the largest proportion of cells showing excitatory responses (40%) compared to inhibited responses (24%) (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: Food-excited neurons showed more sustained activity in response to food compared to shock-excited neurons.
source: Food-excited neurons showed more sustained activity in response to food, and their time to peak activity occurred significantly later than that of shock-excited neurons, likely reflecting the longer time needed to consume food compared to the passive delivery of the shock (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The time to peak activity of food-excited neurons occurred significantly later than that of shock-excited neurons.
source: Food-excited neurons showed more sustained activity in response to food, and their time to peak activity occurred significantly later than that of shock-excited neurons, likely reflecting the longer time needed to consume food compared to the passive delivery of the shock (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The longer time to peak activity in food-excited neurons likely reflects the longer time needed to consume food compared to the passive delivery of the shock.
source: Food-excited neurons showed more sustained activity in response to food, and their time to peak activity occurred significantly later than that of shock-excited neurons, likely reflecting the longer time needed to consume food compared to the passive delivery of the shock (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed differences in timing between food and shock responses.

claim: The maximum Z-score of food-excited neurons was larger than that of shock-excited neurons, indicating that food was more salient for the CeA.
source: Additionally, the maximum Z-score of food-excited neurons was larger than that of shock-excited neurons, indicating that food was more salient for the CeA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and includes an interpretation of the data.

claim: 303 neurons appeared during both appetitive and fear conditioning.
source: To categorize cells as salience or valence encoding, we identified 303 neurons that appeared during both appetitive and fear conditioning (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal registration of neurons across conditioning sessions.

claim: Salience-encoding neurons comprised 15% of the total neurons that appeared during both appetitive and fear conditioning.
source: Salience-encoding neurons (see Methods for detailed definition) were defined as those showing both excited or inhibited responses to food and shock, and comprised 15% of the total neurons (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5B and C.

claim: Valence-encoding neurons represented 65% of the neurons that appeared during both appetitive and fear conditioning.
source: In contrast, valence-encoding neurons were defined as those displaying differential activity to food and shock and represented 65% of the neurons (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5B-E.

claim: 13.5% of valence-encoding neurons showed opposite responses to food or shock.
source: Of these, 13.5% showed opposite responses to food or shock while the remaining 51% showed selective responses to one or the other USs (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5D and E.

claim: 51% of valence-encoding neurons showed selective responses to one or the other USs.
source: Of these, 13.5% showed opposite responses to food or shock while the remaining 51% showed selective responses to one or the other USs (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5D and E.

claim: 20% of neurons that appeared during both appetitive and fear conditioning were categorized as non-responsive.
source: The remaining 20% were categorized as non-responsive.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data analysis.

claim: CeA neurons encode either the valence or the salience of the US, with the valence encoding being more prevalent.
source: These findings demonstrate that CeA neurons encode either the valence or the salience of the US, with the valence encoding being more prevalent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that 65% of neurons encode valence while 15% encode salience.

claim: Only 2% of neurons were classified as salience-encoding based on their responses to CSFood and CSShock.
source: To categorize salience- and valence-encoding neurons based on their responses to CSFood and CSShock, we analyzed the 303 registered neurons recorded during both reward and fear conditioning sessions (Figure 1C and D). Only 2% of neurons were classified as salience-encoding, while 19% were identified as valence-encoding neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data analysis of CS responses.

claim: 19% of neurons were identified as valence-encoding based on their responses to CSFood and CSShock.
source: To categorize salience- and valence-encoding neurons based on their responses to CSFood and CSShock, we analyzed the 303 registered neurons recorded during both reward and fear conditioning sessions (Figure 1C and D). Only 2% of neurons were classified as salience-encoding, while 19% were identified as valence-encoding neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data analysis of CS responses.

claim: CS encoding neurons represent a significantly smaller proportion compared to US encoding neurons.
source: Although representing a significantly smaller proportion of CS encoding neurons compared to the US encoding neurons (CS encoding neurons: salience = 7, valence = 57, not significant = 239; US encoding neurons: salience = 46, valence = 198, not significant = 59; Χ2=215.4, P<0.0001, df = 2), these findings demonstrate that encoding of the valence of the CS is also the predominant response type of the CeA neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of CS and US encoding neurons.

claim: Encoding of the valence of the CS is the predominant response type of the CeA neurons.
source: Although representing a significantly smaller proportion of CS encoding neurons compared to the US encoding neurons (CS encoding neurons: salience = 7, valence = 57, not significant = 239; US encoding neurons: salience = 46, valence = 198, not significant = 59; Χ2=215.4, P<0.0001, df = 2), these findings demonstrate that encoding of the valence of the CS is also the predominant response type of the CeA neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that valence-encoding neurons outnumber salience-encoding neurons for CS responses.

claim: The number of responsive cells during the post-test was less than those observed during conditioning and did not differ from the proportion observed prior to conditioning.
source: The number of responsive cells during the post-test was less than those observed during conditioning and did not differ from the proportion observed prior to conditioning (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing post-test and baseline responses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–J.

claim: The number of CeA neurons excited or inhibited by the food US or shock US was similar using the modified wrapping method and the Wilcoxon sign rank test.
source: The number of CeA neurons excited or inhibited by the food US or shock US was similar to what was identified using the modified wrapping method (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two statistical methods shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: The number of cells responsive to the CSFood was similar using the modified wrapping method and the Wilcoxon sign rank test.
source: Likewise, the number of cells responsive to the CSFood was similar (Figure 5—figure supplement 2J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two statistical methods shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2J and K.

claim: CeA neurons excited or inhibited by the CSShock were more prevalent using the sign rank method compared to the wrapping method (10% excited and 13% inhibited vs. 4% excited and 5% inhibited).
source: CeA neurons excited or inhibited by the CSShock were more prevalent using the sign rank method compared to the wrapping method (10% excited and 13% inhibited vs. 4% excited and 5% inhibited; Figure 5—figure supplement 2L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two statistical methods shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2L and M.

claim: The classification method is not a major contributing factor to the observed results.
source: These marginal differences indicate that the classification method is not a major contributing factor to the observed results and confirm that CeA neurons as a whole are more responsive to the US than to the CS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of two statistical methods showing similar results.

claim: CeA neurons as a whole are more responsive to the US than to the CS.
source: These marginal differences indicate that the classification method is not a major contributing factor to the observed results and confirm that CeA neurons as a whole are more responsive to the US than to the CS.
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing US and CS responses across different analysis methods.

claim: CeA neurons were more responsive to food compared to shock regardless of the conditioning order.
source: Our analysis revealed the following key findings: (i) CeA neurons were more responsive to food compared to shock regardless of the conditioning order (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F), (ii) the ratios of salience-, valence-encoding, and not significant neurons between the two groups were not significantly different (appetitive → fear group US: salience = 22, valence = 115, not significant = 28 vs. fear → appetitive group US: salience = 24, valence = 83, not significant = 31, Χ22 = 3.029, p=0.2199, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F; appetitive → fear group CS: salience = 2, valence = 33, not significant = 109 vs. fear → appetitive group CS: salience = 4, valence = 35, not significant = 120, Χ22 = 0.5126, p=0.7739, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and G), and (iii) the conditioning order did not preferentially recruit CeA neurons based on their topographical locations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and H), indicating that neurons encoding salience or valence were intermingled.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing responses in different conditioning orders shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F.

claim: The ratios of salience-, valence-encoding, and not significant neurons between the appetitive → fear and fear → appetitive groups were not significantly different.
source: Our analysis revealed the following key findings: (i) CeA neurons were more responsive to food compared to shock regardless of the conditioning order (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F), (ii) the ratios of salience-, valence-encoding, and not significant neurons between the two groups were not significantly different (appetitive → fear group US: salience = 22, valence = 115, not significant = 28 vs. fear → appetitive group US: salience = 24, valence = 83, not significant = 31, Χ22 = 3.029, p=0.2199, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F; appetitive → fear group CS: salience = 2, valence = 33, not significant = 109 vs. fear → appetitive group CS: salience = 4, valence = 35, not significant = 120, Χ22 = 0.5126, p=0.7739, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and G), and (iii) the conditioning order did not preferentially recruit CeA neurons based on their topographical locations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and H), indicating that neurons encoding salience or valence were intermingled.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of neuron types across conditioning orders shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, C, F, and G.

claim: The conditioning order did not preferentially recruit CeA neurons based on their topographical locations.
source: Our analysis revealed the following key findings: (i) CeA neurons were more responsive to food compared to shock regardless of the conditioning order (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F), (ii) the ratios of salience-, valence-encoding, and not significant neurons between the two groups were not significantly different (appetitive → fear group US: salience = 22, valence = 115, not significant = 28 vs. fear → appetitive group US: salience = 24, valence = 83, not significant = 31, Χ22 = 3.029, p=0.2199, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F; appetitive → fear group CS: salience = 2, valence = 33, not significant = 109 vs. fear → appetitive group CS: salience = 4, valence = 35, not significant = 120, Χ22 = 0.5126, p=0.7739, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and G), and (iii) the conditioning order did not preferentially recruit CeA neurons based on their topographical locations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and H), indicating that neurons encoding salience or valence were intermingled.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of neuron locations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and H.

claim: Neurons encoding salience or valence were intermingled in the CeA.
source: Our analysis revealed the following key findings: (i) CeA neurons were more responsive to food compared to shock regardless of the conditioning order (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F), (ii) the ratios of salience-, valence-encoding, and not significant neurons between the two groups were not significantly different (appetitive → fear group US: salience = 22, valence = 115, not significant = 28 vs. fear → appetitive group US: salience = 24, valence = 83, not significant = 31, Χ22 = 3.029, p=0.2199, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and F; appetitive → fear group CS: salience = 2, valence = 33, not significant = 109 vs. fear → appetitive group CS: salience = 4, valence = 35, not significant = 120, Χ22 = 0.5126, p=0.7739, df = 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and G), and (iii) the conditioning order did not preferentially recruit CeA neurons based on their topographical locations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and H), indicating that neurons encoding salience or valence were intermingled.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the spatial analysis showing no topographical preference for neuron recruitment.

claim: The response to food before shock (appetitive → fear) was not significantly different from the response to food after the shock experience (fear → appetitive).
source: We found that the response to food before shock (appetitive → fear) was not significantly different from the response to food after the shock experience (fear → appetitive, Figure 5—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing food responses across conditioning orders shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3I.

claim: Similar results were observed for shock, CSFood, and CSShock responses across conditioning orders.
source: Similar results were observed for shock, CSFood, and CSShock responses (Figure 5—figure supplement 3J–L), suggesting that the encoding of positive or negative stimuli in CeA neurons is not influenced by the previous experience with opposing stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing responses across conditioning orders shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3J–L.

claim: The encoding of positive or negative stimuli in CeA neurons is not influenced by the previous experience with opposing stimuli.
source: Similar results were observed for shock, CSFood, and CSShock responses (Figure 5—figure supplement 3J–L), suggesting that the encoding of positive or negative stimuli in CeA neurons is not influenced by the previous experience with opposing stimuli.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no significant differences in responses based on conditioning order.

claim: The CeA is a principally GABAergic structure.
source: The CeA is a principally GABAergic structure, allowing us to image the bulk of CeA neurons through conditional expression of GCaMP in Vgat-Cre mice.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the cellular composition of the CeA.

claim: Imaging the bulk of CeA neurons was achieved through conditional expression of GCaMP in Vgat-Cre mice.
source: The CeA is a principally GABAergic structure, allowing us to image the bulk of CeA neurons through conditional expression of GCaMP in Vgat-Cre mice.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Lens placements largely covered the extent of the dorsal-ventral axis of the CeA.
source: By imaging a total of 10 mice, we were able to achieve lens placements that largely covered the extent of the dorsal-ventral axis of the CeA.
evidence: This claim describes the spatial coverage achieved in the study.

claim: Although the CeA is demarcated by functionally distinct subdivisions and genetically distinct cell types, cells responsive to reward and/or fear were intermingled throughout the structure.
source: Interestingly, although the CeA is demarcated by functionally distinct subdivisions and genetically distinct cell types, we found that cells responsive to reward and/or fear were intermingled throughout the structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of neuron locations and responses.

claim: The definition of salience or valence encoding is often poorly defined, and the terms are frequently used interchangeably.
source: The definition of salience or valence encoding is often poorly defined, and the terms are frequently used interchangeably.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of the literature.

claim: With the exception of a recent study, analysis of specific cell types has not included both an appetitive and aversive stimulus to effectively resolve at the single cell level salience versus valence encoding.
source: Moreover, with the exception of a recent study (Yang et al., 2023), analysis of specific cell types has not included both an appetitive and aversive stimulus to effectively resolve at the single cell level salience versus valence encoding.
evidence: This claim is based on review of the literature and identifies a gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Salience encoding cells were defined as responding in the same direction to both the appetitive or aversive stimulus.
source: For salience encoding, we defined these cells as responding in the same direction to both the appetitive or aversive stimulus as described previously (Gao et al., 2020; Lin and Nicolelis, 2008; Steinberg et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim describes the operational definition used in the study, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Valence encoding cells were defined as cells responding in either the opposite direction to positive or negative stimuli, or selectively responding to one or the other.
source: Valence encoding cells were defined as cells responding in either the opposite direction to positive or negative stimuli, or selectively responding to one or the other (Douglass et al., 2017; Isosaka et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the operational definition used in the study, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Numerous examples of distinct types of salience and valence encoding cells were observed.
source: Although we observed numerous examples of distinct types of salience and valence encoding cells, the majority of neurons within the CeA were similar to what we previously defined as Type 1 valence neurons (Kong and Zweifel, 2021), that is they respond selectively to either the positive or the negative valence of the US.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing different response patterns.

claim: The majority of neurons within the CeA were similar to Type 1 valence neurons, responding selectively to either the positive or the negative valence of the US.
source: Although we observed numerous examples of distinct types of salience and valence encoding cells, the majority of neurons within the CeA were similar to what we previously defined as Type 1 valence neurons (Kong and Zweifel, 2021), that is they respond selectively to either the positive or the negative valence of the US.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data and comparison to prior work.

claim: Increased responsiveness in excited neurons and the number of excited neurons of the CeA to the food US on day 10 compared to day 1 of conditioning was observed, consistent with observations reported for learning-dependent changes in somatostatin expressing neurons of the CeA.
source: Consistent with observations reported for learning-dependent changes in somatostatin expressing neurons of the CeA (Yang et al., 2023), we observed increased responsiveness in excited neurons and the number of excited neurons of the CeA to the food US on day 10 compared to day 1 of conditioning.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Within the last session of Pavlovian appetitive conditioning, enhanced responses in cells inhibited by the food US and CSFood and diminished excitatory response to the CSFood were observed.
source: Within the last session of Pavlovian appetitive conditioning, we observed enhanced responses in cells inhibited by the food US and CSFood and diminished excitatory response to the CSFood.

claim: The enhanced responses in cells inhibited by the food US and CSFood and diminished excitatory response to the CSFood may reflect satiety within the session.

claim: Neurons within the CeA have been shown to play important roles in the regulation of feeding cessation.

claim: A within session decrease in the amplitude of fear US excited cells was observed, consistent with a desensitization of these neurons.
source: We did not record calcium dynamics in CeA neurons across multiple days of fear conditioning; however, we did observe a within session decrease in the amplitude of fear US excited cells consistent with a desensitization of these neurons (Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Numerous studies have identified CeA neurons that respond to the CS following conditioning.

claim: Cells that responded to the CS were observed; however, these responses occurred in a much smaller number of cells compared to the US responding and with a smaller amplitude.
source: We also observed cells that responded to the CS; however, it was evident that these responses occurred in a much smaller number of cells compared to the US responding and with a smaller amplitude.

claim: The observation that CS responses occurred in a much smaller number of cells compared to US responses is consistent with what has been reported previously for specific cell types within the CeA.

evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior literature.

claim: The observation that CS responses occurred in a much smaller number of cells compared to US responses does not discount the previously defined importance of plasticity within these cells for fear-related learning.
source: This is consistent with what has been reported previously for specific cell types within the CeA (Yang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2017) and does not discount the previously defined importance of plasticity within these cells for fear-related learning (Li et al., 2013; Penzo et al., 2014; Sanford et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation that reconciles the current findings with prior literature.

claim: The findings suggest that the CeA as a whole is largely tuned to the valence of the US with approximately equal encoding of both positive and negative valences.

claim: During Pavlovian fear conditioning, alignment of calcium signals to the CSShock revealed that the greatest responses were to the US presentation.
